name: oe-kimi-F-S-P
finalResponse:
Notice, first, that the competitor's lost fifth didn't vanish. They're floating in the market right now, quietly evaluating alternatives. Someone will catch them—it may as well be you. And notice too that the trough isn't really the risk. The trough is the toll. The risk is losing the room halfway across. So perhaps the plan is less about crossing and more about keeping everyone—customers, salespeople, investors—committed to the far bank.

**The floor you already own**
Maintenance revenue is a subscription that dares not speak its name. Customers current on maintenance are already paying recurring money for ongoing value—converting them is closer to re-labeling than selling, nearly revenue-neutral, and it instantly lifts your recurring percentage, which is the number investors will soon care about most. The transition might begin not with a launch but with a quiet campaign: maintenance renewals become subscription conversions, at parity, rate-locked for three years, with credit for recent license purchases. Nothing changes on their invoice. Everything changes on your scoreboard.

**Honor the deed, change the view**
The entitlement objection deserves respect, not argument. They bought the license; it stays theirs—perpetual means perpetual, and any whiff of revocation is how you lose a fifth of your own. The gentler path: freeze the perpetual line at its current version, fully supported, while everything new—collaboration, cloud services, the AI-assisted whatever—flows only to subscribers. The gap widens on its own; you never have to push. And for the genuinely anxious, a fallback mechanism: twelve consecutive months of subscription earns a perpetual license to that version should they ever leave. Ownership anxiety, priced and defused.

**The price of the bridge**
Anchor the annual subscription to the historical upgrade math—roughly what a diligent customer already spent per year—so the honest customer sees continuity, not a shakedown. Then let timing do the persuading: migration credits that decay. Convert this year at maintenance parity; next year at a modest premium; the year after, at list. Deep discounts are tempting as an accelerant, but they set the reference price and deepen the trough without buying durable loyalty—time-limited credits create urgency without poisoning the well. And keep perpetual available, for a while, at a deliberate premium. Some holdouts will pay it, cushioning the trough, and its mere existence makes the subscription look reasonable by comparison. Choice architecture, not coercion.

**The trough is partly an accounting rumor**
GAAP revenue craters; cash behaves differently. Annual and multi-year prepayments mean the cash trough runs shallower than the P&L trough—deferred revenue quietly becomes the real story. Depth is also a dial, not a fate: force conversion fast and it's deep and short; let the perpetual tail linger at premium prices and it's shallow and long. Choose deliberately—and say aloud which you chose.

**Compensation is the real migration**
Business models don't migrate; salespeople do. If a $150k perpetual deal pays more than a $50k-a-year subscription, your strategy is a memo. Make the economics indifferent, or better: commission on full first-year contract value at the old rate, a kicker for multi-year prepay, spiffs per converted installed-base account, a clawback if the customer churns inside twelve months. Then decay the perpetual commission on a published schedule until selling it becomes economically irrational. One caution: a comp redesign layered on a revenue trough is precisely when your best people get poached. A two-quarter comp floor costs little and buys the loyalty you'll need. It may also be worth splitting the motion—hunters hunt, converters convert—so neither job is done badly.

**Telling the market before the market tells you**
Name the trough before it arrives: expected depth, duration, exit velocity, in public, with a bridge model. Then change the scoreboard—ARR, percentage recurring, net revenue retention, deferred revenue, installed-base conversion rate—and guide on those, because the old number will only frighten people. Show cohort economics: what a converted customer is worth versus a holdout. With the board, pre-agree the milestones that define "on track," so the strategy isn't re-litigated each quarter by whoever read the revenue line first. And use the competitor openly: their failure was one of *manner*, not direction—abrupt versus graceful—and your plan is that difference. The well-known parable from the creative-software world ended in a multiple re-rating, but only because the trough was announced, owned, and then beaten modestly, quarter after quarter.

**The gift floating in the market**
Someone else's orphaned fifth is shopping. A displacement program—generous cross-grade pricing, migration tooling, white-glove onboarding—might be the cheapest growth you ever buy. Their churn, your ARR.

---

As for sequencing—the grand cutover is the obvious answer, which is perhaps reason enough to be suspicious of it. One segment, one region, one product line: run the conversion playbook there, learn where the entitlement friction actually lives, then scale what survived contact.

And a question worth leaving on the table: of your installed base, how many are already behaving like subscribers—current on maintenance, upgrading on rhythm—and simply haven't been asked? That number is your real starting point. It may be considerably larger than the fear suggests.
